catalog_quote: Se puede saber que en el segundo caso la partícula es ligada por la colocación de la fuerza de la voz que en quechua recae en la penúltima sílaba: a.'li.cag / NO 'a.li # cag [Toliver p. 52] ... Cabe anotar que los datos (vea el apéndice) corresponden principalmente a las variedades que se hablan en el departamento de Huánuco, especialmente las variedades de Ambo-Pasco, Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha (MYL) y Huamalíes. Las conclusiones del presente trabajo se aplican principalmente a esas variedades [Toliver p. 50] ... En la mayoría de las variedades centrales del quechua, el acento se asigna a la penúltima sílaba. Por ejemplo: [aywá:pis] /aywa-:-pis/ 'yo también voy' [aywaša:píta] /aywa-ša-:-pita/ 'desde que fui'. En esos dialectos, la vocal larga que funciona como marcador de primera persona se acentúa cuando está en posición final de palabra: [aywá:] /aywa-:/ 'voy' [Weber & Landerman p. 25] ... En la variedad del Huallaga y algunas otras variedades, también se acentúan las vocales largas finales que tienen otra procedencia: [manárax] ~ [manará:] /mana-raq/ 'todavía no' ... Según el análisis V: = [V][V], la regla de colocación del acento podría formularse así: "Acentúese la penúltima vocal". ... En todo caso, los últimos dos ejemplos muestran que, para estas variedades la colocación del acento es una regla que no trata a las palabras que terminan en vocal larga como a las que terminan en consonante. [Weber & Landerman p. 26]

new_statements.translation: One can tell that in the second case the particle is bound by the placement of the stress, which in Quechua falls on the penultimate syllable: a.'li.cag, NOT 'a.li # cag [p. 52]. It should be noted that the data (see the appendix) correspond mainly to the varieties spoken in the department of Huánuco, especially the Ambo-Pasco, Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha (MYL) and Huamalíes varieties. [p. 50]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (suffixes and bound particles count as part of the word, so stress shifts rightward as suffixes are added). The companion article in the same volume (Weber & Landerman 2008: 25-26) states the Central Quechua rule the same way and adds that a word-final long vowel (the 1st-person marker -:) takes the stress, i.e. effectively penultimate mora.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Toliver. Weber & Landerman (pp. 25-26, same file) note that in Central Quechua the word-final long vowel marking 1st person is stressed, and that Huallaga 'and some other varieties' also stress other final long vowels (e.g. manará: ~ manárax); which of these applies to MYL is not specified.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (a nickname/word-formation argument: bound particle cag inside the word vs. free particle); passing statement about 'Quechua' in an article whose data are explicitly from Ambo-Pasco, MYL and Huamalíes; not a dedicated phonology of qvm.
new_statements.identity_note: No dedicated grammar or phonology of qvm exists in Glottolog or in any repository reached. The quoted statement is Toliver's (SIL Peru) remark about 'Quechua' inside an article whose data are explicitly from the Huánuco varieties Ambo-Pasco (ambo1252), Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha (marg1254) and Huamalíes (huam1248); it is therefore a first-hand but not qvm-exclusive statement. Weber & Landerman 2008 (same volume, pp. 25-26) give the same penultimate rule for 'most Central Quechua varieties' with the final-long-vowel (1st person) exception; Weber 1996/2008 sec. 23.6 gives 'penultimate mora' for Huallaga Quechua (hual1241), a different Glottolog language. The Bean 2008 and Marsch 2008 articles in the same volume are qvm-specific (distrito de Margos) but silent on stress.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final [...] In the Quechua I dialects stress is maintained in word-final position when the long vowel morpheme referring to first-person subject or possessor is immediately followed by a word boundary. (Length oppositions not connected with the first-person morpheme are normally neutralised in word-final position, in which case stress is regularly assigned to the penultimate syllable.) [...] Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976).

It adds the Quechua I first-person final-long-vowel exception, the interjection/emphatic exception and the Ancash/Cajatambo contrast, none of which the catalog records. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field; this…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word (a word-delimitation cue). In Quechua I varieties (to which this lect belongs) a word-final long vowel marking first-person subject/possessor keeps the stress on the final syllable (e.g. wási 'house' vs wasí: 'my house'); other final long vowels are neutralised and the word is stressed on the penult. Interjections and emphatic expressions may be stressed word-finally. Non-penultimate systems (initial stress, syllable-structure sensitivity) are ascribed to quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo, not to the Huánuco group.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final stress on the first-person long-vowel morpheme (quantity-insensitive); interjections and emphatic expressions; elision-derived final stress in Tarma / northern Junín; phonemic final vs penultimate stress in Pacaraos; word-initial and weight-dependent stress in quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976).
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken 2004 describe Quechua as a family and Quechua I as a group; the Margos-Yarowilca-Lauricocha lect is not named anywhere in the book (probes for Margos, Yarowilca, Lauricocha, Dos de Mayo, Yacha, Ambo-Pasco all 0 hits). In the book's dialect survey (Torero's groups, c. pp. 185-186) the lect's area belongs to 'Alto Pativilca-Alto Marañón-Alto Huallaga', which 'includes the remainder of the Quechua-speaking area of the department of Huánuco' (after Marañón and Huamalíes are assigned to the Huaylas-Conchucos group); the book's Huánuco sources are Weber 1989 (Huallaga) and Toliver MS 1987 (Pasco). The example wási / wasí: 'my house' is Huanca, not Huánuco.
